title: How many steps does one image need? Tested on two models, and even big 2MP images don't break
summary: Both models hit their quality ceiling early: Z-Image Turbo gives a finished image in 1 step, and Flux2 caps out at 8 steps, saving 60% of the time vs the official default of 20; big 2MP (1216×1632) images generate natively without breaking, and Z-Image takes just 9.2s.
tags: Z-Image makes an image in 1 step

stats: How many steps does Z-Image need?
1 step already gives a complete finished image (3.1s); from 2 to 16 steps there's no visible difference — 4 steps for drafts and 8 for finals is enough, more won't be better
How many steps does Flux2 need?
Quality caps out at 8 steps; 8 vs 12/20/32 shows no difference: ▮ 6.0s (8 steps) vs ▮▮▮ 18.1s (32 steps) look identical — picking 8 steps saves 60% of the time vs the official default of 20

Yes: under the same seed (the number that controls generation randomness), the sha256 (a fingerprint that proves files are bit-for-bit identical) of the 8-step image matches last round's sweep image exactly
Yes, without breaking: at 1216×1632 (2MP), Z-Image takes just 9.2s and Flux2 39.3s, and the detail keeps growing over 0.6MP
Does last round's best 0.6MP setting still hold?

Corrected on the image side: 0.6MP was the value-for-money turning point, not the capability ceiling — for bigger images go straight to 2MP; unchanged on the video side: still bound by H3's hard 768 short-edge limit, so its best setting stands
findings: Z-Image Turbo lives up to its name: step count barely affects time (3-6s), so you can't pick a wrong setting
Flux2's official default of 20 steps is too conservative: at 8 steps the quality looks identical by eye and you save 60% of the time — 8 steps is the best setting
For big static images, generate 2MP directly (Z-Image takes just 9s); no need to make a small image first and upscale it afterwards
